cover.alt: The React API Every UI Library Secretly Depends On

content: Every React dev has built a modal or a tooltip at some point. If you've ever built one yourself by changing the position to absolute or changing the z-index to 99999, you've probably faced clipping, layering bugs, or the modal ending up behind something else on the page instead of being in front of everything. But the moment you use a Modal component from a UI library, it just works, smooth, no fighting anything.

content.text: Ever stopped to ask why? What is it that the people building these libraries know, that you don’t?

content: Here’s the actual requirement underneath all of this, We want something to render in front of everything else in our React app.

But here’s the catch. Whatever component you write for that modal is still a React component, and it renders inside your React application like everything else. That makes it a node, a child sitting deep inside the DOM tree, wherever it happens to be nested. So it’s really hard for it to escape its parent tags and render in front of everything.

content.text: So how do UI libraries solve this problem?

content: Portals solve exactly the problem we just walked through. createPortal is a React API that lets you render something completely outside your actual React application in the DOM. Here’s how it works:
When you spin up a new React project, your index.html has a div with id="root", and that HTML file references /src/main.jsx as a script.
Inside main.jsx, React calls createRoot, passing in that same root div as the target. From there, it calls .render() on it and renders your entire React application inside that div with id="root"

The createPortal API breaks that rule. The DOM node or HTML element you pass into it escapes from whatever containers it may be in, no matter how deep it was written in your component tree. Instead of landing inside root like everything else, it renders directly into the document, as a direct child of the HTML document's body, rendering above the root div in which the rest of the React app is rendered.

And it’s still a React node under the hood. The JSX you render into a portal acts as a child node of the React component that renders it. The child can access the context provided by the parent tree, and events bubble up from children to parents according to the React tree.
Let’s actually build a Portal. We’ll use it to render a Modal component in front of our React app.

content.text: Step 1: Add a div above root

content: Open your index.html, and add a new div right above the root div. This is where our portal content will actually land.

content: Now build a Modal component that uses createPortal to render its children into that modal-root div instead of wherever it's called from.

content.text: Step 3: Use it like any other component

content: Here’s the part that feels a bit like magic the first time you see it. You use Modal exactly like you'd use any other component, nested wherever it makes sense in your JSX.

content: Here’s the part that feels a bit like magic the first time you see it. You use Modal exactly like you'd use any other component, nested wherever it makes sense in your JSX.

Even though <Modal> is written right inside App, its actual output lands in modal-root, sitting next to root in the DOM instead of buried inside your app's markup. It’s placed directly into the document body, above the root div, sitting exactly where we wanted it.
That’s really it. A small API, but one that quietly changes how you think about rendering in React.

Now that you’ve seen it in action, go check the source code of any UI library, shadcn, Radix, MUI, doesn’t matter which one. Open up their Modal or Dialog component, and you’ll find createPortal sitting right there, doing exactly what we just built by hand.
